analysis.title: US Economic Notes: What you need to know for the week ahead (30 October 2026)
key_insights: Tuesday's midterm elections and Friday's October employment report are the main events of the week. DB says polling suggests Democrats are likely to flip the three seats needed for a House majority, and their odds of netting four Senate seats have risen steadily since the primaries.

Trump's approval rating of about 36% would imply a loss of nearly 50 seats for Republicans (House and Senate combined), based on that relationship over prior cycles. Senate polling in the races that decide control is still within the margin of error, and in 2024 Trump won at least five of the seven core toss-up states. DB therefore sees the Senate as a much closer call than the House, and a result may take several days if control comes down to a few seats.

A Democratic Senate could affect Trump's ability to confirm executive branch appointments, including at the Fed. DB expects neither party to hold a veto-proof majority, so the fiscal outlook is unlikely to change meaningfully.

The most consequential legislative period is the lame duck session between the election and the first week of January. Republicans will likely try a party-line reconciliation bill in the coming weeks that could add substantially to defense spending and possibly address the debt limit, which must be dealt with before late summer or fall of next year.

Federal government funding runs out on December 11, so a continuing resolution needs bipartisan support to avoid a shutdown. This week's Treasury Quarterly Refunding Announcement is also in focus, and DB points to its fixed income preview 'Refunding preview: Keeping options open'.

DB forecasts October nonfarm payrolls at +55k (vs +29k previously) and private payrolls at +55k (vs +46k), moving closer to their three-month averages of 51k and 54k. If the forecast is close, the unemployment rate stays at 4.2%.

DB expects hours worked steady at 34.4 and average hourly earnings to rebound to +0.3% from +0.1%. Its payroll proxy for nominal compensation growth should slip a tenth to 4.1% year over year, which DB still calls supportive of solid consumer spending growth.

The rest of the week's data sets the tone for Friday. DB forecasts manufacturing ISM 54.8 (vs 54.5), services ISM 55.1 (vs 54.9), ADP +75k (vs +90k) and University of Michigan sentiment 45.7 (vs 48.0). Business sentiment has diverged from consumer attitudes over the past year.

ADP on Wednesday is expected to have the most influence on market expectations for Friday's payrolls because the two series' growth rates are significantly correlated. Fed officials will watch Tuesday's JOLTS for deviations in the hiring, quits and layoff rates, which have been steady for the past year.

The Fed held at last week's FOMC meeting, and Chair Warsh reiterated the likely need for further tightening. Barring meaningful downside misses, DB expects this week's employment data to reinforce market expectations of another rate hike at the December 9 FOMC meeting.

Fedspeak may show how far officials expect to tighten. NY Fed President Williams has stressed data trends and endorsed one more hike by year-end, while Dallas Fed President Logan said unwinding last year's insurance cuts is the minimum needed to bring policy to an appropriate level.

Governor Cook will attend a closed-door, transcribed hearing at the White House on Thursday before a presidential committee of inquiry. The committee is to recommend to the President whether there is 'cause' for her removal.

macro_indicators.interpretation: DB expects payrolls to move back toward the three-month average of 51k, which would support expectations of a December rate hike.
A rise toward the 54k three-month average would be consistent with steady hiring.
An unchanged rate would leave no labor market reason for the Fed to pause its tightening bias.
A rebound in monthly wage growth, with payroll-proxy compensation growth slipping a tenth to 4.1% y/y, which DB calls still supportive of consumer spending.
Business sentiment stays strong and has diverged from weak consumer sentiment.
A forward-looking read on business sentiment ahead of Friday's payrolls.
Expected to have the most impact on market expectations for nonfarm payrolls given the correlation between the two series.
Consumer attitudes remain weak while business sentiment is strong.

risk_factors: The Senate outcome is a close call, and a result could take several days if control comes down to a few seats in either chamber.
A Democratic Senate could complicate confirmation of executive branch appointments, including at the Fed.
A government funding lapse on December 11 if no bipartisan continuing resolution passes.
